title: After the Midterms, Republicans Weigh a Loss Their Own Side Calls Not Historic
excerpt: Democrats flipped at least 40 House seats and seven Senate seats. A Republican strategist argues petrol prices, not collapse, explain the defeat — and that the veto still gives Trump the last word.
body:
• Democrats flipped at least 40 House seats and seven Senate seats, taking both chambers; the new Congress convenes on January 3, 2027.
  • Republican strategist Tim Constantine argues the defeat was driven mainly by the Iran war's effect on petrol and grocery prices, and that the loss is not historic by post-war midterm standards.
  • President Trump keeps the veto — overriding one needs two-thirds of both chambers — and Senate control by Democrats makes any Supreme Court vacancy a much harder fight.
  • Before January, Republicans still hold both chambers for a 55-day lame-duck session, with House leadership elections on Tuesday and a December 11 government funding deadline.

Democrats flipped at least 40 House seats and seven Senate seats in Tuesday's midterm elections, a result Republican strategist Tim Constantine, writing in Al Jazeera, describes as a clear message that much of the country is unhappy with its direction — but not, he argues, a historic defeat for the party in power.

All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats were on the ballot. The flips included states Republicans had treated as safe ground: Texas, which had not elected a Democrat in a statewide race for more than 30 years, and Kansas, which had not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. In Maine, Susan Collins, chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee and a senator for 30 years, was voted out. Dozens of House races were still being counted, so the Democratic tally may grow.

What drove the loss

Constantine argues the defeat was driven less by the Iran war itself than by its economic effects, above all petrol prices, which feed into the cost of food and groceries because nearly every product is delivered by road. He notes that only 14 percent of Americans think Congress is doing a good job, and that both President Trump and Vice President JD Vance have already acknowledged the war and its economic effects as the primary reasons for the loss — an admission he says will help the party move on.

"The GOP suffered a loss, but it is hardly a historic one. A party in power has always been held to account in the midterms."

— Tim Constantine, Republican strategist, in Al Jazeera

His historical yardstick: Truman's Democrats lost 55 House and 12 Senate seats in 1946, Eisenhower's Republicans lost 48 House and 13 Senate seats in 1958, Republicans gained 54 House seats under Clinton in 1994, and Obama's Democrats lost 63 House seats and six Senate seats in 2010. Presidents who took such losses, including Clinton and Obama, came back; writing the Republican Party's obituary now, he argues, is premature.

The 55 days Republicans still have

Defeated Republican lawmakers return to Washington on Monday with 55 days of majority left, according to The Wall Street Journal. Republicans hold leadership elections in the House and Senate on Tuesday: Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking the minority leader job, setting up a contest between Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, while John Thune is expected to remain the Senate Republican leader. Federal funding lapses on December 11, and Senate Republicans are expected to focus on confirming as many of Trump's judicial nominees as possible before January.

Two years of divided government

From January 3, Democrats will control every committee and virtually every vote in both chambers, restoring congressional oversight and, Constantine writes, making investigations of Trump and his team — and talk of impeachment — routine. Against that, Trump retains the veto, which takes two-thirds of both the House and the Senate to override, and Constantine expects him to use it regularly if Democrats push an agenda he calls too far left. For Indian Americans and for Indians watching US immigration policy, the practical point is the same one that applies to every other file: committee control changes oversight and legislation, but executive actions still run through the White House and the agencies.

The 2028 question

Constantine calls predicting the 2028 Republican nominee now a fool's errand. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are the obvious names, but he raises the problem of Trump fatigue: if voters have grown weary of Trump, anyone tied to his administration may be baggage rather than an advantage, and an outsider — a governor or a figure from outside the administration — could generate the enthusiasm the party needs. Until Republicans settle whether they need a new messenger, different policies, or a different way of exercising power, the succession contest is also a contest over what the party becomes.
